title: Why do the poles get less sun?
hook: The North Pole gets less sunlight in a year than the equator. What causes the gap?

doesNotKnow: that it is the angle of the sunlight, not extra distance from the Sun, that cuts their yearly sunlight to about two fifths of the equator's

misconception: The poles are cold because they are farther from the Sun.
objective: The learner can say that the North Pole gets about 41% of the equator's yearly top-of-atmosphere sunlight, and that the cause is the angle (the same beam spread over more ground), not its at most 6,371 km of extra distance.

claims.text: Over a year the North Pole gets about 41% of the equator's sunlight per square metre at the top of the atmosphere (51.5 N 67%, 60 N 57%, 30 N 88%).
claims.source: Daily-mean insolation Q = (S0/pi)(h0 sin(lat) sin(dec) + cos(lat) cos(dec) sin(h0)) (Berger 1978) averaged over a circular orbit in 3,600 steps: 415.5, 365.2, 277.0, 236.3 and 172.3 W/m^2 at 0, 30, 51.5, 60 and 90 N (pole/equator 0.415). Section `insol-annual` of company/domains/briefs/checks/geography-wave-j.mjs; re-run by the builder (scratchpad insol.mjs) and computed in Demo.tsx. Hartmann 2016 (Global Physical Climatology, ch. 2) shows about 417 and 173 W/m^2 (not opened by the builder).

claims.text: The pole is at most 6,371 km farther from the Sun, 0.004% of the way.
claims.source: Earth mean radius 6,371.0088 km (IUGG; EARTH_RADIUS_KM in src/kit/geo); 1 AU = 149,597,870.7 km (IAU 2012 resolution B2). At equinox the pole is R (1 - cos 90) = R farther along the Sun line than the sub-solar point: 6,371 / 149,597,870.7 = 0.0043%. Readout shown to 3 decimals: 0.004%. Sources not opened by the builder.

claims.text: That extra distance is worth less than 0.01% of the light.
claims.source: Flux falls as 1/r^2: 1 - (1 AU / (1 AU + 6,371 km))^2 = 0.0085% (section `insol-annual`).

claims.text: Near the poles the same beam lands on more ground, so each square metre gets less: at equinox noon the lit ground is 1/cos(latitude) times the beam's width (x1.61 at 51.5 N, x2.00 at 60 N), and at the pole the beam grazes the ground.
claims.source: Geometry of a parallel beam meeting a sphere at angle (90 - latitude) at equinox noon. Section `insol-annual` prints 1.00, 1.15, 1.61, 2.00. Drawn in Demo.tsx as the lit arc under a fixed-width band.
Scope statement on the stage: the picture is equinox noon; the yearly share is above the air. The card makes no claim about climate zones (that needs temperature data).

recall.question: Name the reason a square metre near the pole gets less sunlight in a year than one at the equator.
options: The same beam is spread over more ground
The pole is farther from the Sun
recall.why: Low sunlight spreads one beam over more ground. The pole's extra distance changes the light by under 0.01%.
